football_evidence.question: Can Iowa’s pass rush get to Drake Lindsey?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Iowa, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.0 of the 3.6 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Minnesota has the ball (the run game against the run defense): Minnesota’s offense averages 3.6 yards per carry, and Iowa’s defense allows 3.8 yards per carry (FBS average 5.1).

When Minnesota has the ball (big plays on the ground): Minnesota’s offense turns 3.7% of its runs into explosive gains, and Iowa’s defense gives up explosive gains on 2.7% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).
When Minnesota has the ball (third down): Minnesota’s offense converts 29.8% of its third downs, and Iowa’s defense allows opponents to convert 38.8% of their third downs (FBS average 39.7%).

When Iowa has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Iowa’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 13.8% of its runs, and Minnesota’s defense stops 15.4% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.3%).
contradicting: In his last two games (Michigan and Ohio State), Brown averaged 5.8 yards per attempt, against 7.9 in his three games before that.
EdgeDesk’s position-group ratings put Minnesota’s pass defense No. 38 nationally and Iowa’s No. 79.
quarterbacks: Drake Lindsey has completed 128 of 196 passes (65.3%) for 1,350 yards, 6.9 yards per attempt, 10 touchdowns and 5 interceptions in six games for Minnesota, and has been sacked on 2 of 198 dropbacks.
Hank Brown has completed 78 of 124 passes (62.9%) for 850 yards, 6.9 yards per attempt, 5 touchdowns and 1 interception in five games for Iowa, and has been sacked on 4 of 128 dropbacks.
Jeremy Hecklinski has completed 31 of 50 passes (62.0%) for 386 yards, 7.7 yards per attempt, 4 touchdowns and 1 interception in four games for Iowa, and has been sacked on 1 of 51 dropbacks.

model: Iowa’s defense has to come out ahead in the pass-rush matchup: it sacks the quarterback on 10.6% of opponent dropbacks, against an offense that has allowed a sack on 1.4% of its dropbacks.
Iowa’s defense has to come out ahead on long runs: it gives up explosive gains on 2.7% of opponent runs, against an offense that turns 3.7% of its runs into explosive gains.
Iowa’s defense has to come out ahead on the ground: it allows 3.8 yards per carry, against an offense that averages 3.6 yards per carry.
Iowa’s quarterback situation has to settle: Hank Brown has taken 47% of Iowa’s recent dropbacks and Jeremy Hecklinski 39%.
market: Minnesota’s offense has to keep winning in the pass-rush matchup: it has allowed a sack on 1.4% of its dropbacks, and Iowa’s defense sacks the quarterback on 10.6% of opponent dropbacks.
Lindsey keeps producing at his season rate (65.3% completions, 6.9 yards per attempt, 10 TD, 5 INT).
